newsitem.title: GERMANY: Intel, SES form satellite - PC venture.
newsitem.headline: Intel, SES form satellite - PC venture.

text.p: Luxembourg's Societe Europeenne des Satellites and computer chip maker Intel Corp have formed a venture to deliver video and other multimedia services direct to personal computers via satellite, the two said on Wednesday.

The venture, European Satellite Multimedia Services S.A. (EMS), would give media companies a way of broadcasting digital multimedia content to home and business PCs much faster than telephone lines, the partners said at the CeBIT trade fair.

"We want to use Europe's well-developed satellite network to support high-speed data transmission to personal computers," said Intel Europe chief Hans Geyer. "Tens of millions of people will soon be able to communicate by computer. The problem is that getting information is limited by data transmission speed."

EMS's satellite service, due to begin operating later this year, would be able to transmit 10 megabytes of data -- enough for a short video clip -- in 2.2 seconds. Today's fastest ISDN telephone lines would require 22 minutes.
EMS was backed with initial investments of about $15 million, with Luxembourg's SES holding a majority share, although others are expected to join as the venture takes off, the companies said.
EMS would provide its service to magazines, television broadcasters and cable companies who develop media services for PCs and the Internet, said Romain Bausch, SES director general.
"You can imagine the contents of a VCR tape being sent to a PC over our network," Bausch said.

The partners plan first to develop services aimed at businesses that already use satellites in corporate networks. Home users would need add-in cards costing about $200 to link their PCs to a standard 50-centimetre satellite dish.
With 16 percent of European homes -- or 26 million -- now equipped with satellite dishes, Europe is ripe for such a service, Bausch said.

Since cable TV systems could also use EMS's Astra Net to provide multimedia content to PCs, the venture has the potential to reach another 46 million homes, he said. In total EMS could reach about 41 percent of European homes.
The number of satellite-equipped homes was expected to rise to 45 million by 2006, Bausch added. "There is a tremendous opportunity."
Intel also said it expected opportunities for similar satellite services to open up in Asia and North America over the next several years, but it had no plans now for other ventures.
SES, with a network of six satellites, provides data transmission and networking services to large businesses. It plans to launch four more satellites over the next two years.
